title: The Last Postcards
premise: When restaurant critic Beatrix Dravenmoor hears an unrecorded song on the radio — one her late mother wrote and swore never to release — she returns to the crumbling Dravenmoor estate, where her estranged brother Julian is preparing the house for demolition. Among her mother's belongings Beatrix finds a shoebox of unsent postcards revealing that the song was co-written with a woman named Odile, erased from every family record, and that the demolition is Julian's way of burying a truth about their father's death. As Beatrix tracks down Odile's daughter, she must choose between protecting the family name her brother is desperate to preserve and telling the truth that will free them both; in the end she publishes the postcards, loses her column but regains her sense of taste, and stands with Julian on the empty lot as the song plays from a passing car.
about_author: Sable Reyes is the pen name of a former food writer who left restaurant journalism after a decade of reviews she no longer believes. She lives near a decommissioned lighthouse and writes about families, memory, and the things we archive instead of say.

chapters.title: The Numb Tongue
chapters.summary: Beatrix files another glowing review for food she cannot taste, hiding her condition from her editor. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: quiet shame — a woman professionally fluent in pleasure she no longer feels.

chapters.title: A Song With No Name
chapters.summary: Driving home, Beatrix hears a radio session featuring an unfamiliar melody her mother hummed only in private — a song supposedly never written down. She calls the station; the band credits a 'traditional arrangement.' POV: Beatrix. Beat: vertigo, the past intruding on the present.

chapters.title: The Letter From the County
chapters.summary: Julian writes: Dravenmoor House will be demolished in six weeks; come collect what you want. Beatrix hasn't spoken to him since their father's funeral. POV: Beatrix. Beat: dread mixed with obligation.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Beatrix arrives at the decaying estate; Julian is brisk, defensive, eager to hurry her along. She notices he has already cleared their mother's music room. POV: alternating Beatrix/Julian. Beat: friction between siblings performing civility.

chapters.title: The Shoebox
chapters.summary: Behind a loose panel Beatrix finds forty postcards, all addressed to her, none sent, written in her mother's hand over thirty years. The earliest mentions 'O.' POV: Beatrix. Beat: hunger — the first real appetite she's felt in years.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: fifteen years ago, Beatrix's first review, and the moment after her father's death when she stopped tasting. POV: Beatrix (past). Beat: grief revealed as the root of her numbness.

chapters.title: Odile
chapters.summary: The postcards name Odile Marchand — co-writer of the song, erased from family albums, photos cut out but not discarded. Beatrix begins searching records online. POV: Beatrix. Beat: detective's thrill shadowed by betrayal on her mother's behalf.

chapters.title: Julian's Ledger
chapters.summary: Julian POV: he discovers someone searched the attic; his demolition timeline isn't just development — it's erasure of evidence about the night their father died. Beat: fear hardening into control.

chapters.title: The Daughter in Lyon
chapters.summary: Beatrix reaches Camille, Odile's daughter, by phone. Camille is cold: her mother died believing the Dravenmoors stole everything, including the song. POV: phone call, dual interiority via Beatrix. Beat: guilt inherited secondhand.

chapters.title: The Postcard Dated the Last Winter
chapters.summary: A postcard reveals their father didn't die accidentally — he fell during a confrontation over selling the song to a publisher without Odile's consent. Their mother saw it and said nothing. POV: Beatrix. Beat: the floor giving way beneath family myth.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Site Fence
chapters.summary: Beatrix confronts Julian at the property; he admits he knows what the house holds and wants it buried before developers' surveys. He accuses her of never having loved any of them enough to stay silent. POV: Julian. Beat: loyalty weaponized against truth.

chapters.title: The Column
chapters.summary: Beatrix's editor demands a career-retrospective feature; writing it, she realizes every review was a postcard she never sent either. She drafts something honest for the first time. POV: Beatrix. Beat: tentative self-recognition.

chapters.title: Camille Arrives
chapters.summary: Camille comes to see the house her mother described in letters — and finds it half-gutted. Her fury forces Beatrix to admit how much the family concealed, including from herself. POV: Camille. Beat: outsider's clarity cutting through sibling code.

chapters.title: The Music Room Reopened
chapters.summary: Beatrix pries open the sealed music room: sheet music in two hands, her mother's and Odile's, the song complete — lyrics about a house that eats its daughters. POV: Beatrix. Beat: awe and horror entwined.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: The developer offers Julian a bonus for early clearance; simultaneously a music publisher, tipped off by the radio session, offers real money for the song — if provenance can be verified. Julian asks Beatrix to sign away her claim. POV: Julian. Beat: corruption dressed as pragmatism.

chapters.title: Forgiving the Stranger
chapters.summary: Reading the final postcards, Beatrix understands her mother as a whole person — complicit, silenced, loving. She forgives the stranger in the photographs, which means refusing to keep forgiving the living lie. POV: Beatrix. Beat: grief transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: Demolition Eve
chapters.summary: Machines arrive at the fence line. Julian finds the music room emptied overnight; Beatrix has the score, the postcards, and Camille's testimony. He threatens legal action; she threatens publication. POV: alternating. Beat: standoff at maximum tension.

chapters.title: The Song Played Twice
chapters.summary: Climax: at the county hearing on the demolition permit, Beatrix plays the recording of the radio session and reads the postcards aloud. Julian, cornered, finally confesses what he found in the cellar years ago — and why silence felt like protection. POV: alternating. Beat: truth detonating the family's foundation.

chapters.title: Rubble and Seed
chapters.summary: The demolition proceeds anyway — but on Beatrix's terms: she donates the salvageable music room contents to an archive crediting Odile Marchand equally. Julian signs nothing, says nothing, stays. POV: Julian. Beat: loss without lies, for the first time.

chapters.title: The Review That Tasted Like Something
chapters.summary: Beatrix publishes the honest retrospective and is let go from her column. Eating alone at a diner, salt on her lips, she tastes food again — imperfectly, but truly. POV: Beatrix. Beat: restoration through relinquishment.

chapters.title: Postcards, Finally Sent
chapters.summary: Beatrix mails the original postcards to Camille, adding one of her own addressed to her mother, care of the archive. Camille replies with a photograph: Odile and Beatrix's mother laughing, uncut. POV: Beatrix. Beat: inheritance redefined as shared memory.

chapters.title: The Empty Lot
chapters.summary: Epilogue: spring. Beatrix and Julian stand on the razed foundation where wildflowers have already seeded. A passing car plays the song, now properly credited. Neither speaks; both stay until it ends. POV: alternating. Beat: reconciliation without absolution — loyalty rebuilt on truth.
